subChunks.title: PL/pgSQL Functions and Stored Procedures
subChunks.hookHtml: Some logic belongs in the database — near the data, atomic with transactions, reusable by multiple clients. Stored functions and procedures are that tool.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
SQL function (simple)

CREATE FUNCTION add_xp(p_apprentice_id INT, p_amount INT)
RETURNS void AS $$
  UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + p_amount WHERE id = p_apprentice_id;
$$ LANGUAGE sql;

-- Call:
SELECT add_xp(1, 100);

PL/pgSQL function (with logic)

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION promote_if_ready(p_id INT)
RETURNS TEXT AS $$
DECLARE
  v_xp    INT;
  v_rank  TEXT;
BEGIN
  SELECT xp, rank INTO v_xp, v_rank FROM apprentices WHERE id = p_id;

  IF v_xp >= 6500 AND v_rank != 'Archmage' THEN
    UPDATE apprentices SET rank = 'Archmage' WHERE id = p_id;
    RETURN 'Promoted to Archmage';
  ELSE
    RETURN 'Not ready';
  END IF;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

Stored procedure (PostgreSQL 11+)

Functions return a value; procedures do not (they are called with CALL). Procedures can manage transactions (COMMIT/ROLLBACK inside the procedure).

CREATE PROCEDURE promote_batch()
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE apprentices SET rank = 'Adept' WHERE xp >= 2000 AND rank = 'Apprentice';
  UPDATE apprentices SET rank = 'Mage'  WHERE xp >= 4000 AND rank = 'Adept';
  COMMIT;
END;
$$;

CALL promote_batch();

When to use stored functions

  • Complex business logic that must be atomic with the transaction
  • Shared logic used by multiple clients/services
  • Triggers (next lesson) — trigger functions are always PL/pgSQL

When NOT to use stored functions

  • Business logic that needs testing — stored procedures are harder to unit test
  • Logic that involves external services, HTTP calls, or file I/O
  • Frequently changing business rules — application code is easier to deploy

storyBeats.text: Three different services all need to apply the same promotion logic. Duplicating it in each service is fragile.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: A function lives in the database. All callers share the same logic, the same transaction context. Change the function and all callers update immediately. But keep complex, frequently-changing business logic in your application — it is easier to test and deploy there.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Function design

Write a PL/pgSQL function award_badge(p_user_id INT, p_badge_name TEXT) that: checks if the badge already exists for the user, inserts it if not, and returns 'awarded' or 'already_earned'. Sketch the function body.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Describe a scenario where putting logic in a stored function is better than in application code, and a scenario where application code is better. Justify each.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Better in a stored function: an XP award operation that must update apprentices.xp, insert into xp_audit, and check for rank promotion — all atomically in one transaction. Three different services (web API, background job, admin CLI) call this logic. A function ensures consistency and atomicity regardless of the caller.

Better in application code: a recommendation algorithm that ranks quests by user history, difficulty, and time of day. This logic changes weekly as the team refines it, needs unit tests against mock data, and has complex conditional logic. Deploying a stored function change requires a database migration; deploying application code change is a simple push.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between a SQL function and a stored procedure in PostgreSQL, and describe when you would choose a stored procedure over a function.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a function and a stored procedure in PostgreSQL?
options: Functions return a value and are called in SELECT; procedures do not return a value and are called with CALL — procedures can also manage transactions internally
Procedures support PL/pgSQL; functions only support SQL
Functions can modify tables; procedures cannot
questions.answer: Functions return a value and are called in SELECT; procedures do not return a value and are called with CALL — procedures can also manage transactions internally
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL functions return a value (scalar, record, table, or void) and are invoked in expressions or SELECT. Procedures (added in PG11) are called with CALL and can issue COMMIT/ROLLBACK inside the procedure body.

questions.prompt: In PL/pgSQL, what does `SELECT col INTO v_var FROM t WHERE id = 1` do?
options: Assigns the value of col for the matched row into the local variable v_var
Creates a new table named v_var
Throws an error — INTO is not valid in PL/pgSQL
questions.answer: Assigns the value of col for the matched row into the local variable v_var
questions.explanation: SELECT ... INTO is the PL/pgSQL way to fetch a single row's values into local variables. If the query returns no rows, the variable is NULL. If it returns multiple rows, the last row wins (or raise an exception if STRICT is used).

questions.prompt: When should business logic be in a stored function rather than application code?
options: When the logic must be atomic with the database transaction and shared by multiple clients with no single application layer
When the logic calls external APIs
questions.answer: When the logic must be atomic with the database transaction and shared by multiple clients with no single application layer
questions.explanation: Stored functions run inside the database transaction — they have full ACID guarantees and avoid race conditions. They are ideal for cross-cutting logic (audit logging, balance enforcement) shared by multiple services.

questions.prompt: A team debates: put promotion logic in a stored function vs application service. The logic changes monthly. Which is better and why?
options: Application service — deploying a code change is faster and easier than deploying a database migration that modifies a stored function
Stored function — database functions are always faster
Stored function — application services cannot handle transactions
questions.answer: Application service — deploying a code change is faster and easier than deploying a database migration that modifies a stored function
questions.explanation: Frequently-changing logic belongs where deployment is easiest — application code. Changing a stored function requires a database migration (potentially with downtime, rollback complexity). Unit testing stored functions is also harder. Reserve stored functions for stable, transaction-critical logic.
